title: Sector Lens: Positioning Notes for Fintech, Healthcare, Legal, Enterprise SaaS, Gov/Defense
content:
Purpose and scope:
Quick working brief that surfaces a ‘sector lens’ for messaging experiments and sales collateral. Focus is on what matters to engineering and platform buyers (not marketing slogans) — economics, reliability, compliance controls, and operational levers. This is intentionally pragmatic: hypothesis-first statements we can A/B test in landing pages, datasheets, and AE scripts.

High-level positioning thesis (shared across sectors):
- Core claim: Redwood turns LLM risk/cost variability into predictable, instrumented inference — same API, measurable unit economics, deploys on hosted/dedicated/private.
- Key proof pillars: predictable latency (SLOs), cost controls (batching/quantization suggestions), observable regressions (evals + alerting), and deploy flexibility (VPC/on-prem options).

Vertical-specific framing (one-paragraph briefs + buyer hooks):
1) Fintech (payments, wealth, lending platforms)
- Pain: model drift causing regulatory flags, opaque inference costs at peak volumes, and data isolation needs.
- Message: Predictable pricing + private deploy options reduce runway risk for productionizing LLM features; audit trails and evals reduce compliance overhead.
- Buyer persona: Platform eng + Head of Data/ML; procurement cares about committed spend.
- Tactical assets: cost-per-transaction calculator, compliance checklist for model governance, latency SLO case study for millisecond-sensitive flows.

2) Healthcare (clinical decision support, patient triage)
- Pain: PHI handling, auditability, clinical safety and hallucination risk.
- Message: Private control plane + KMS/HSM integrations + eval-driven regression alerts give compliance teams confidence to pilot clinically adjacent features.
- Buyer persona: Head of engineering (healthcare platform), Privacy officer, Clinical safety reviewer.
- Tactical assets: security architecture diagram, PHI dataflow playbook, small-scale pilot template.

3) Legal (contract review, discovery)
- Pain: confidentiality, deterministic outputs for audit, tight access controls.
- Message: Dedicated pods + strong RBAC + model pinning for reproducible outputs; rollouts with canary/fallbacks preserve throughput under heavy loads.
- Buyer persona: Legal ops + IT security + Solutions engineers.
- Tactical assets: contract redaction demo, reproducibility/test-suite for model rollouts, partner integration checklist for eDiscovery tools.

4) Enterprise SaaS (B2B apps adding LLM features)
- Pain: unpredictable token spend from heavy user adoption, inconsistent latency across regions, difficulty benchmarking model quality at scale.
- Message: Redwood Optimize suggestions (batching, KV caching, quant profiles) plus regional routing let product teams control unit economics while keeping response quality.
- Buyer persona: Product engineering lead and platform team; finance hooks into commit sizing.
- Tactical assets: ROI model for feature toggles, latency/cost heatmap by region, migration playbook from single-hosted endpoints to dedicated pools.

5) Gov/Defense (classified, regulated deployments)
- Pain: air-gapped networks, procurement-heavy purchasing, long security review cycles.
- Message: Private/on-prem deployment model, HSM integrations, and audit-ready telemetry shorten assessment windows and provide a path to certifiable deployments.
- Buyer persona: Systems integrator, government program manager, security accreditation leads.
- Tactical assets: non-prod evaluation kit, compliance artifact templates, procurement-friendly procurement brief.

Competitive notes (how to tilt against common alternatives):
- Cloud-managed endpoints that emphasize model parity: emphasize economy + predictable throughput; show per-transaction cost comparisons at realistic batch sizes.
- Self-hosted runtimes: emphasize developer experience + observability + rollout safety (we provide pattern + tooling, not just kernels).
- Large closed-model APIs: emphasize deployment flexibility and data isolation; price/latency comparisons at scale.

Topline one-liners (testable variants):
- Variant A (economics-first): "Make LLM unit costs predictable — deploy hosted, reserved, or private without rewiring your app."
- Variant B (reliability-first): "Latency SLOs and automatic fallbacks keep your AI-powered features live under load."
- Variant C (compliance-first): "Private control planes, audit logs, and HSMs for regulated AI deployments."

Go-to-market experiments (prioritized):
1) Vertical landing page with cost calculator + one concrete case study (Fintech) — measure demo requests and MQL conversion.
2) Short technical whitepaper (SaaS) focusing on batching/kv-caching ROI; gated download collects contact + workload profile.
3) Security playbook for Healthcare with a checklist; syndicate through channel partners and measure inbound from compliance roles.
4) Gov-oriented evaluation kit (air-gapped demo); coordinate with solutions engineering to run two PoCs in next quarter.

Open questions and risks to validate:
- Pricing transparency vs competitive price elasticity: how much detail can we show without washing out negotiated enterprise deals?
- What benchmarks best predict customer-perceived quality across verticals (latency percentiles, rejection rates, hallucination metrics)?
- How to standardize a minimal compliance artifact set for pilot handoffs (healthcare + gov intersection)?

Immediate next steps (owners and timing):
- Build Fintech landing + cost calculator (owner: Priya, due: 2025-03-21).
- Draft SaaS technical whitepaper (owner: Evan, due: 2025-03-28).
- Run internal tabletop for Healthcare security playbook with applied-ml & security (owner: Marcus, meeting: 2025-03-10).

Notes to self / room for iteration:
- Keep language testable and concrete; avoid abstract "trust" claims without operational artifacts.
- Focus initial collateral on engineering artifacts (diagrams, runbooks, sample configs) because buyer is technical.
- Keep a short "what success looks like" checklist for each vertical to guide AE conversations.

End of brief.

Document history: working draft — will convert sections into page templates and AE cheat-sheets after first experiment results are in.
